nameStory: The word 'plum' comes from the Latin 'prunum,' which the Romans borrowed from Greek. These trees have been cultivated for over 2,000 years, with the 'domestica' part of their scientific name literally meaning 'of the house' - telling us these are the homegrown plums that have lived alongside humans for millennia.
description: Domestic plums are small to medium-sized deciduous trees that typically reach 15-20 feet tall with a rounded, spreading crown. They're the source of most plums you'd find in grocery stores, including sweet European varieties and tart damsons. In spring, these trees burst into clouds of white or pale pink flowers before the leaves emerge, creating a stunning early-season display. The smooth, oval fruits ripen in late summer in shades of purple, blue, red, or yellow.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Smooth-skinned oval fruits with a waxy bloom that rubs off on your fingers, containing a single large pit that doesn't easily separate from the flesh when you bite into it

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Clusters of 2-5 white or pale pink flowers with five rounded petals, appearing before the leaves in early spring and filling the air with a sweet, honey-like fragrance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-4 inches long with finely toothed edges and a smooth, slightly glossy surface that feels firm to the touch, arranged alternately on branches

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Dark gray to brown bark that becomes furrowed and slightly scaly with age, often showing horizontal lines called lenticels that feel slightly raised

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Small tree with a short trunk and spreading branches that often form a broad, rounded crown, frequently producing suckers from the base

habitat: Domestic plums are found around old homesteads, abandoned farms, and occasionally escaped into woodland edges and disturbed areas throughout New England. They prefer well-drained soils and full sun, often persisting long after the original plantings as testament to their hardiness. You're most likely to encounter them near stone walls, old cellar holes, or in rural areas where they were once cultivated.

seasonality.spring: Showy white or pink flowers bloom in April or early May before leaves emerge, creating spectacular displays that attract early pollinators like bees and flies.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage of oval, toothed leaves provides dense shade while fruits develop from green to their final colors by late summer.
seasonality.fall: Ripe fruits hang heavy on branches in August and September, while leaves may turn yellow before dropping, and you might smell the sweet scent of fallen fruit fermenting on the ground.
seasonality.winter: Bare branching pattern is visible along with dark bark and small, pointed buds, while dried fruits may persist on branches into early winter.

funFact: Domestic plum trees are essentially botanical time capsules - some varieties growing wild in New England today are the exact same cultivars that European colonists brought over 300 years ago, still faithfully producing fruit at long-abandoned homesteads where families once lived and farmed.
confusionNotes: Domestic plums are most easily confused with their wild relatives like beach plums or American plums, but domestic plum fruits are typically larger and sweeter, and the trees grow taller with less thorny branches. Remember: if it's growing near old human settlements and the plums are grocery-store sized, it's likely the domestic species.
contextualKnowledge: Many 'plum' species aren't actually Prunus domestica - this species specifically refers to European plums including greengages and damsons. What Americans often call 'Japanese plums' are actually a different species entirely, and our native beach plums and American plums are their own distinct species with different characteristics.
compareHints: Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees. Unlike cherries in the same genus, plum fruits are typically larger with a more pronounced waxy bloom and the pit clings more tightly to the flesh. Beach plums stay much smaller and grow in coastal areas, while domestic plums prefer inland locations near human habitation.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
